mainEntity.name: How long should sensitivity last after a new crown is fitted?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mild sensitivity following crown placement is normal and typically settles within two to four weeks. The tooth has undergone preparation, which can temporarily irritate the inner pulp tissue. During this period, brief sensitivity to cold, heat, or pressure is not unusual. If your sensitivity is severe, not improving, or worsening beyond this timeframe, it is advisable to contact your dentist. Every patient responds slightly differently, so there is no fixed point at which sensitivity must stop — what is most important is the direction of change.

mainEntity.name: Can a crown cause long-term nerve damage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Crown preparation involves reshaping the natural tooth, which places some stress on the pulp. In most cases, the pulp recovers without issue. However, in a minority of cases — particularly where the tooth was already compromised before the crown was placed — the pulp can become irreversibly inflamed over time. This is not a failure of the procedure but a biological response. If irreversible pulpitis develops, root canal treatment may be recommended. Your dentist will monitor and assess any persistent symptoms to determine whether further treatment is needed.

mainEntity.name: Why is my crown sensitive to cold but not to heat?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cold sensitivity that resolves quickly after the stimulus is removed is often associated with reversible pulpitis or dentine exposure — both of which may not require immediate intervention beyond monitoring. Sensitivity to heat, or a prolonged response to cold lasting more than 30 seconds, can sometimes indicate a more advanced stage of pulp inflammation. These distinctions are clinically useful, which is why your dentist will ask specific questions about the character and duration of your sensitivity during assessment. It is not always possible to self-diagnose the cause based on the type of sensitivity alone.

mainEntity.name: What happens if sensitivity beneath a crown is left untreated?

acceptedAnswer.text: This depends entirely on the cause. Mild sensitivity from a high bite or temporary pulp irritation may resolve on its own. However, if the underlying cause is progressive — such as failing crown margins allowing bacterial ingress, or irreversible pulpitis — delaying assessment can allow the condition to worsen. Decay beneath a crown, for instance, is more straightforward to address in its early stages. If in doubt, it is always preferable to have symptoms assessed sooner rather than later, as early intervention is generally associated with simpler management options.

mainEntity.name: Is it possible for decay to develop under a dental crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Whilst the crown itself does not decay, the natural tooth structure beneath it can still be affected by dental caries if bacteria penetrate the crown margin. This is more likely if the cement seal breaks down over time, or if there is a marginal gap. Decay beneath a crown may not always present obvious symptoms initially, which is why routine dental examinations and X-rays are important for monitoring crowned teeth over time. Good oral hygiene at the gum line around the crown helps reduce the risk of marginal decay.

mainEntity.name: Should I use a sensitivity toothpaste for crown sensitivity?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sensitivity toothpastes may provide some relief for crown-related cold sensitivity, particularly if gum recession or exposed dentine is a contributing factor. However, they are not a substitute for professional assessment. If sensitivity is persistent or worsening, using a sensitivity toothpaste whilst waiting for a dental appointment is reasonable, but it should not be used as a long-term strategy to mask symptoms that may warrant clinical attention. Always inform your dentist that you have been experiencing sensitivity, even if it has reduced, as this information is clinically relevant.
